comments.text: > how come people with sliding rulers and navigation computers 'knitted' by local grannies have lost 0 Saturn rockets. The fuck? NASA lost people in production hardware multiple times. [LINK] [LINK] "The damaged third-stage engine failed to restart for trans-lunar injection... Despite the engine failures, the flight provided NASA with enough confidence to use the Saturn V for crewed launches..." [LINK] [LINK] [LINK] Here's a fun one: They tested the Saturn crew escape system. The booster was supposed to blow up, and demonstrate the crew would survive... but the test went wrong , and it blew up early , when it shouldn't have. The crew abort worked, so test failed successfully . [VIDEO]

comments.why: Example of a failed test that still validated the design.
comments.text: > If a test flight doesn't achieve the testing objectives, that's a failure. Incorrect. Examples: [VIDEO] is a Saturn launch abort test that failed. It failed in a way that they were able to determine that intended test would have worked, though. [LINK] also failed to achieve its objectives; "Despite the engine failures, the flight provided NASA with enough confidence to use the Saturn V for crewed launches; a potential third uncrewed flight was cancelled." All that aside, SpaceX was quite clear that the latest Starship test had multiple objectives, and that "successfully splashdown near Hawaii" was deemed quite unlikely. It successfully demonstrated a number of items, including fairly critically the launchpad changes.

comments.author: hoorayimhelping
comments.why: Illustrates launch escape tower on a rocket.
comments.text: Red is kerosene, blue is liquid oxygen, orange is liquid hydrogen, the fuel that looks like fire is solid fuel (think compressed gunpowder). Left to right: Saturn V, Space Shuttle, Falcon 9 Heavy, SLS (still under construction). 2:22, you hear Neil Armstrong say "inboard cutout," that is the center engine shutting off to limit the thrust, and therefore G-forces the astronauts felt. As fuel ran out, the rocket stack would weigh less and so the rocket would push harder. By the time the main engine cutoff, the Saturn V was pulling 4 and a half Gs. Also, just noticed the SLS keeps its launch escape tower (the big needle on the top of the rocket - see this: [VIDEO] ) - this wouldn't happen in a real flight. The flight plan calls for ditching than when it's not longer useful - you can hear the Apollo 11 call saying, "tower jettisoned."

comments.author: msl
comments.story: The death of a weather satellite as seen by SDR
comments.why: Rocket breaking up from excessive roll rate.
comments.text: Satellites usually need to point their solar panels and high-gain antennas properly in order to stay powered to be able to communicate with ground stations, although this particular satellite seems to have been unable to use its high-gain antenna anyway and relied on an omnidirectional one anyway. Another issue would be thermal management as it is possible that not all parts of the satellite were designed to deal with direct sunlight. I would be more worried about all the sensors, though. The days of secondary electron conduction tubes [1] might be long over, but many instruments still prefer not to be pointed directly at the sun. Speaking of those other sensors, spinning the satellite would mean pointing all of them away from where they are supposed to be looking – not necessarily a net win. Finally, trying to spin the satellite at anything approaching 360 RPM might end up dramatically shortening the mission [2]. [1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO] EDIT: In case you do not feel like watching the video, [2] shows a Little Joe II rocket ( [LINK] ) breaking up due to an excessive roll rate (around 56 RPM) ( [LINK] ).

comments.author: ceejayoz
comments.story: Musk says SpaceX knows what caused the latest rocket failure
comments.why: Saturn escape test that survived an out-of-control rocket.
comments.text: Spinning's entirely possible to survive. The Saturn missions tested it (and it was a really good test - something went wrong and the rocket actually went out of control) - [VIDEO] A tumble should be fairly trivial to detect and fire only when the capsule's in its upwards pointing portion of the tumble. Plus, you'd only be firing into the ground if you're pretty early in the launch - the Dragon launch abort only sent it up a kilometer or so. Finally , the launch abort is pretty sensitive - deviating not far off the right direction should trigger it, before a full-on tumble.

comments.author: hcrisp
comments.why: Apollo escape system test surviving a rocket failure.
comments.text: Apollo's launch escape system was tested using a rocket called Little Joe II, which started spiraling unexpectedly due to a gyro problem causing the rocket to fail. Fortunately the escape system worked as intended. [1] [VIDEO]
